\section[investigar]{investigar — to investigate}

\label{lesson:ES-C521-investigar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the victim, then the Spanish for the investigation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: investigar}
\textbf{investigar} — \textquotedblleft{}to investigate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La policía investiga el caso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police are investigating the case.}
\end{quote}

It takes \emph{gu} before \emph{e}: \emph{investigué}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{investigar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{investīgāre} 'to track, to search after' (EtymDB), built on \emph{vestīgium} 'a footprint'. To investigate is to follow the footprints.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{investigar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{investigar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{investigar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the victim, then the Spanish for the investigation, then say \emph{investigar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does investigar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To investigate\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pista]{la pista — the clue, the lead; the track}

\label{lesson:ES-C521-pista}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the investigation, then the Spanish for to investigate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la pista}
\textbf{la pista} — \textquotedblleft{}the clue, the lead; the track\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La policía no tiene ninguna pista.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police do not have any leads.}
\end{quote}

It also means a track or court: \emph{una pista de tenis}, \emph{la pista de baile}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pista} was borrowed from Italian \emph{pista} 'a track, a beaten trail' (EtymDB). A clue is the trail you follow.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la pista}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la pista}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la pista}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the investigation, then the Spanish for to investigate, then say \emph{la pista} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la pista mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The clue, the lead; the track\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la prueba]{la prueba — the proof, the evidence; the test}

\label{lesson:ES-C521-prueba}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to investigate, then the Spanish for the clue.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la prueba}
\textbf{la prueba} — \textquotedblleft{}the proof, the evidence; the test\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No hay pruebas contra él.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is no evidence against him.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Una prueba} is also a test: \emph{una prueba de inglés}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{prueba} is built on \emph{probar} 'to test, to try', which is inherited from Latin \emph{probāre} 'to test, to prove' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la prueba}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la prueba}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to investigate, then the Spanish for the clue, then say \emph{la prueba} again
\end{itemize}

\section[averiguar]{averiguar — to find out}

\label{lesson:ES-C521-averiguar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the clue, then the Spanish for the proof.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: averiguar}
\textbf{averiguar} — \textquotedblleft{}to find out\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quiero averiguar qué pasó.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I want to find out what happened.}
\end{quote}

It takes \emph{ü} before \emph{e}: \emph{averigüé}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{averiguar} is usually traced to Late Latin \emph{verificāre} 'to show to be true', built on \emph{vērus} 'true'. To find out is to get at the truth.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{averiguar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{averiguar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the clue, then the Spanish for the proof, then say \emph{averiguar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does averiguar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To find out\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[sospechar]{sospechar — to suspect}

\label{lesson:ES-C521-sospechar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the proof, then the Spanish for to find out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sospechar}
\textbf{sospechar} — \textquotedblleft{}to suspect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nadie sospechaba de él.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Nobody suspected him.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sospechar de alguien} — to suspect someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sospechar} is inherited from Latin \emph{suspectāre} 'to look up at, to suspect' (EtymDB), built on \emph{suspicere} 'to look up at'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
